glance_takeaway: The page is about a research project called 'murmur' testing whether near-free, natural-reverb-flavoured audio augmentation can beat spending on a bigger backbone, for classifying 6,200 clips across 34 long-tailed bird species. Its main message: the hypothesis is only partially supported — the best augmentation stack lifts validation macro-F1 from 0.612 to 0.671 (+5.9 points) at negligible compute, but the gain concentrates in common species and barely reaches the rare tail. A run of six experiments shows pitch/time-stretch actually fell below the no-augmentation floor, and the noise-mix step's +0.002 was within seed noise (±0.006), i.e. a null.

strengths: Exceptional caveat fidelity: the null result, seed noise (±0.006), the exp-03 regression, the deep-tail −0.01, and even 'the cheaper-than-a-bigger-backbone half of the bet (H2) is still asserted, not shown' are all explicit — the page actively refuses to oversell.
The standfirst compresses the honest verdict (0.612→0.671, gain concentrated in common species, two augmentations removed) so nearly all required takeaways land above the fold.

Visual encodings are honest and load-bearing: SVG coordinates were checked against stated values and match exactly in both charts; annotations explain mechanism (why the dip, why the null) rather than decorate.
weaknesses: The 70/15/15 stratified split (F3) is effectively absent — only the ~930-clip test-split fragment survives in a footnote.

Dataset texture is thinned: clip format (5 s mono, 32 kHz) and the imbalance statistics (11 species < 80 clips, median ~120, top-8 = 52%) are dropped, so a collaborator can't gauge how deep the tail problem is beyond five example species.

Fig 1's x-axis spaces six dated experiments evenly despite uneven calendar gaps (16 to 25 days), a mild ordinal-vs-time dishonesty; and the 'one thing changed per step' semantics of '+ noise mix' depends on reading the caption.
